internshipsAndProjects.name: Eous AR-Car
internshipsAndProjects.role: 1st Place Winner at Stanford's Immerse the Bay 2025 Hackathon
internshipsAndProjects.description:
Developed an RC Car remotely controlled from Augmented Reality (AR) glasses.

The user would control the car with gestures recognized by the AR glasses, which would send the commands to a Raspberry Pi which controlled the car via an Arduino microcontroller. In addition, the user could see a live feed from the car in the display of the AR glasses.
The user could also talk with ChatGPT on the car, which would allow the user to ask general questions or command actions, like playing music on Spotify.

This project was created on the XREAL Sponsored Track at Stanford's Immerse the Bay Hackathon with Feolu __, Ryan Chen, and Tyler Wong.

internshipsAndProjects.name: Stellantis
internshipsAndProjects.description:
Developed a CAPL script to measure the fault detection fidelity of the high speed ADAS camera component, by hijacking CAN signals using Vector CANalyzer to simulate setting DTCs (error codes for vehicle components).

Simultaneously, ran controlled experiment to measure automatic longitudinal control by controlling CAN signals of acceleration/deceleration using Vector CANoe.

internshipsAndProjects.name: Capoom
internshipsAndProjects.role: Software Engineering Intern, via Perot Jain Tech Lab at Mcity Program
internshipsAndProjects.description:
Developing method for automatic 3D Gaussian Splat model creation of UofM's Mcity as an inexpensive, lightweight testbed for autonomous vehicle companies to train and test their vehicles

Established the data collection pipeline using Lucid Cameras with Arena SDK and implemented 3D modeling using Gaussian Splatting techniques through Reality Capture and Post Shot software to create detailed small-scale models. I explored two hierarchical Gaussian splatting methods - CityGaussianV2 and Hierarchical 3D Gaussians - to effectively scale up these models while maintaining detail quality and minimizing computational resources.

internshipsAndProjects.name: Constant Therapy Health
internshipsAndProjects.description:
Constant Therapy, a digital health therapeutic technology company that develops tablet-based software to help stroke patients relearn everyday skills through digital-therapy tasks. Worked on the Task progression Visualizer, which is a ReactJS web page that analyzes how patients progress through tasks, and from that, tasks can be reworked to optimally help patients. My project was to make the Visualizer work on the company's newest version of data, which required me to make significant changes to the backend JavaScript and Python code.

Improved their speech recognition / grammar detection with LLMs system for stroke patients. I fine-tuned Meta's Wav2Vec Automatic Speech Recognition model to recognize phonemes rather than full words, which had a false negative rate 4x lower than Google's speech recognition model. I also worked on a Large Language Model to detect the accuracy of grammar in a patient's response. My work is now currently in the Constant Therapy app, being used by patients globally.

internshipsAndProjects.name: HELM Learning
internshipsAndProjects.description:
I created HELM Learning, a platform for middle and high school students to teach classes to K-12 students worldwide for free. This platform connected 4,000+ students to 90+ student-teachers. I built the back-end system using a Python Flask app, which I hosted on an AWS EC2 instance that connected to a MySQL Database.

To accommodate for HELM's growing number of classes, I created a Machine Learning Recommendation Algorithm to suggest students new classes they should sign up for based on their previously shown interests in certain subjects. This was implemented into the current sign up page after a student signs up for a class.

This algorithm used an MLP classifier to create a model for each class, which would output the probability of a student taking that class. Once all models have given an output, the top 3 probabilities are taken, and those classes are recommended to the student. A random 4th class was added as a control to know if the algorithm worked or not

Presented at the Massachusetts State Science and Engineering Fair, receiving 4th place.

researchProjects.title: Go Fetch: Safe Mobile manipulation in a Gaussian Splat
researchProjects.description:
Currently using Vision Language Action models (VLAs) to develop generalist robots that can perform a wide range of tasks, such as grasping, pushing, and pulling objects.

Last semester, I worked on a novel pipeline for safe mobile manipulation by implementing scene representation through 3D Gaussian Splatting, which efficiently generates detailed, manipulable 3D models from RGB-D images.

  • I integrated object detection capabilities combining GroundingDINO for zero-shot target identification and Meta's Segment Anything Model for precise object segmentation, allowing the system to identify specific clusters of Gaussians associated with target objects.
  • I established grasp detection functionality using AnyGrasp to generate optimal gripper positions for the Fetch robot to safely manipulate objects in novel environments.
  • I leveraged ORBSLAM3 to process continuous camera feeds, track features across frames, and generate accurate camera positions that were essential for creating the initial point cloud used to produce Normalized Gaussians for scene representation.

Together, my contributions formed the foundation for a computationally efficient and safe autonomous system capable of understanding scenes, identifying objects, and calculating appropriate grasping positions without prior environment knowledge.

researchProjects.title: Visual Confirmation System for Autonomous Vehicles
researchProjects.description:
The aim of this project was to create a secure visual confirmation system for autonomous vehicles (AVs) communicating with road-side units (RSUs), like a traffic light. For an RSU to verify the identity of an AV, the AV flashes its headlights in a specific sequence. My project was to detect the recognition of this sequence using Python. I worked solely, as a paid intern under the supervision of Post-doc Dajiang Suo and Professor Sanjay Sarma of MIT.

  • This system first detects a vehicle using a YOLOv8 Computer Vision model, and cropping the frame to just the vehicle.
  • It then detects whether the vehicle's headlights were on or off per frame, by turning each RGB cropped image into a binary image, showing where the bright regions are.
  • I evaluated several approaches that have been previously studied (including a few that use machine learning), but developed a new approach that uses binary images, so as to maximize the detection accuracy and minimize processing latency.
  • The system finally determines whether the sequence of headlight flashes follows the sequence originally sent to the AV, accounting for possible errors.

Biggest challenge: process identity while the vehicle is moving through a street intersection in less than 1 second & to work in a lot of situations: variable lighting, different types of vehicles, different shapes of headlights, etc.

researchProjects.title: Digital Twin for Pedestrian Safety Warning at a Single Urban Traffic Intersection
researchProjects.institution: Center for Smart Street Scapes, Columbia University
researchProjects.description:
The aim of this project was to create a phone application and a backend server that warns pedestrians at street intersections about potential collisions with vehicles. I solely created this, with the guidance of PhD student Yongjie Fu and Professor Sharon Di, both of Columbia University.

I used Python and React Native to develop this system. The app uses React Native as a framework for the front-end user interface, and communicates via MQTT messages to a Python backend server.

The app ran the following steps:

  • Location coordinates are sent to, and processed by the backend server.
  • Backend server constructs a trajectory that predicts where the pedestrian is likely to be in the next 5 seconds.
  • Backend Server receives data about where vehicles currently are, and where their predicted trajectories will be over the next 5 seconds.
  • Based on this data, the server predicts if there is likely to be a collision between pedestrians and each vehicle.
  • As appropriate, the server sends back warnings to the pedestrian's phones.

The app was optimized for multiple devices of any make and model to connect to it, and maximized accuracy and minimized latency in harsh situations (i.e., weak connection).

Paper published at the IEEE IV 2024 Intelligent Vehicles Symposium here.
